artboards.title: Following a Raised link — what the merge is FOR
True side by side — drawn, then counted

annotations.text:
The brief

Sales invoices and purchase invoices go on one screen, as two lenses: Sales | Purchases.

They are not merely symmetrical. Invoicing a customer's order RAISES a supplier bill for every supplier used on it — one object, two documents.

The case is already written in index.html

Beside the two helpers that walk the link, the file says:

"An order, the invoice it becomes and the purchase invoice it generates against a supplier are one thing moving through the business. The data has always known that. The screens did not. THREE TABS NAMED AFTER TABLES, ONE OBJECT."

purchaseInvoicesForOrder() and orderForPurchaseInvoice() exist. The sales row ALREADY carries its "Raised" links. Nothing here is invented — what is new is where pressing one lands.

What following that link costs today

revealPurchaseInvoice() has to: change tab, type the number into the OTHER screen's search box, widen its date range, drop its voided filter, and raise a toast — and its own comment explains why all four are needed.

Getting back means undoing every one by hand, because the sales list you left is gone.

One screen, one filter bar: the press becomes a lens switch, and Back is one press to a list that never moved.

One filter bar, because it already is one

Search-first placement, the same seven date presets, the same Hide voided, the same .inv-f classes — the two screens are already identical here, and index.html says so in a comment on the second one ("as on Invoices").

Two copies of one bar is precisely what made the cross-screen link expensive.

What each lens keeps

Sales keeps its three orderings, its select-all and bulk-void, and the printed sheet as the one accent — it is the thing a person walks the yard with.

Purchases keeps its checks band and its rail, and its list print stays a ghost: the accent there belongs to the bill you open, which is index.html's own reasoning.

So the strips differ, and that is right — they measure different things and the lens name says which you are on.

You asked for side by side first — so here it is, built rather than dismissed.

Each register gets 578px once the 220px rail is off. The band on the artboard counts what has to go: four of the sales register's eight columns including the bulk-void, and on the buying side What it was for, Dated, the 304px rail and the whole checks band — which has nothing on the sales side to sit opposite it.

And the "Raised" links stop meaning anything: with both lists already on screen, pressing one can only scroll the other.

This app also has a standing law against it. Movements was pulled OUT of Inventory for being "a whole second console stacked under the first" — this is that fault turned on its side.

A third option the data refuses

One row per TRANSACTION — the order, with its sales invoice and its supplier bills nested under it — is the truest reading of "one object". I did not draw it because generatePurchaseInvoiceForRestock() sets quoteId: null.

A shop's restocks have no order behind them at all. That view would orphan them, and restocks are most of the buying. It could only ever be a third lens, never the whole screen.

The one thing I could not decide for you

Which rail section it lives in. Invoices is under Sell; Purchase invoices is under Buy. One screen cannot be in both.

The artboards put it under Sell and leave Buy with the four screens about CHOOSING what to buy and from whom — Buy loses a row and gains the keywords.

That breaks a claim admin-nav.test.js currently makes ("buying stock is one job across three screens"), which is a decision to take deliberately rather than patch.

The phone is its own design

The lens is full width under the name, 44px a side — the same move the Price registry and Inventory lenses make.

Eight desk columns become a card each: who, the figure that matters, then the document and its date.

The "Raised" links keep their place under the name. On a phone they are the only way to reach the other half of a transaction without going back to the list — which makes them worth more here than on the desk, not less.
